title: How to use Lunar Site Planner

lines.text: Welcome to Lunar Site Planner! This short video shows you how to use it, one step at a time.
The app answers two simple questions about landing on the Moon.
Will the lander get enough sunlight to make power? And can it talk to Earth by radio?
The screen has four main parts.
On the left, you choose where to land.
lines.label: 1 · Choose a site

lines.text: In the middle, you see the Moon, and a timeline of the coming weeks.
lines.label: 2 · Moon and timeline

lines.text: On the right are the results for your site.
lines.label: 3 · Results

lines.text: And across the top, you set the date and time.
lines.label: 4 · Date and time

lines.text: To pick a site, just click a name in this list.
You can also click anywhere on the 3D Moon, or type a latitude and longitude in this box.
lines.say: You can also click anywhere on the 3D Moon, or type a latitude and longitude in this box.

lines.text: We'll start with the Shackleton connecting ridge: a high ridge right next to the lunar south pole.
The results panel tells you how things look at your site, at the chosen moment.
The Power card shows how many watts the solar panels make. A green “Meets load” means there's enough power to run the lander.
lines.say: The Power card shows how many watts the solar panels make. A green, Meets load, means there's enough power to run the lander.

lines.text: The Earth link card shows whether the lander can radio Earth. Green means yes. Red means Earth is hidden behind the terrain.
Underneath, two countdowns tell you when the Sun will set, and when Earth will next rise or set.
Now let's try a different spot: the floor of Shackleton crater, about twenty kilometres away.
The crater floor sits in permanent shadow. It never sees the Sun, so solar power drops to zero.
A short distance can make all the difference. That's why landing sites are chosen so carefully.
This sky chart shows what you'd see standing at the site, looking all the way around you.
The grey shape is the real skyline of hills and crater walls, measured by a NASA laser in orbit.
The yellow line is the Sun's path, and the blue line is Earth's. When they're above the grey, they're visible.
Below, the window summary adds it all up, like how much of the time the site is sunlit.
Conditions change over time, so set the date and time up here. All times are in UTC.
lines.say: Conditions change over time, so set the date and time up here. All times are in U.T.C.

lines.text: Use the plus and minus buttons to step by an hour or a day, or press Play to watch time move.
The timeline at the bottom shows the coming weeks at a glance.
Each coloured row is something the lander needs: sunlight, power, Earth in view, a ground station, and a working radio link.
A coloured bar means it's available. A gap means it's not.
Click or drag on the timeline to jump to any moment, and use these buttons to show fifteen days, a lunar day, three months, or a whole year.
Use these tabs to switch between the 3D Moon and a flat map of the south pole.
The map can colour every spot by how much sunlight it gets. Yellow areas get the most sunlight, so they're the best-lit places to land.
And “Stand here: Sun” shows the view from the lander itself, looking toward the Sun.
lines.say: And, Stand here Sun, shows the view from the lander itself, looking toward the Sun.

lines.text: Found a good option? Press “Add to compare” to save this site and date.
lines.say: Found a good option? Press, Add to compare, to save this site and date.

lines.text: The Compare panel lines your options up side by side.
“Schedule slip” tests landing one, two or three months later. “Find nearby alternatives” looks for better-lit spots close by.
lines.say: Schedule slip tests landing one, two, or three months later. And, Find nearby alternatives, looks for better-lit spots close by.

lines.text: The best and worst values are highlighted, and you can export everything as a spreadsheet.
Stuck on a word? Click any question-mark button for a short definition.
Or turn on Learn mode for plain-language explanations right inside the results.
The Spacecraft button lets you change the lander: its solar panels, how much power it uses, and its radio.
That's it! You can replay this video at any time with the Video tutorial button at the top. Happy landing!
